\sphinxstylestrong{Examples:} Power grid depends on communication network, supply chains, cyber\sphinxhyphen{}physical systems.


\subsubsection{When to Use Multilayer Networks}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:when-to-use-multilayer-networks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use multilayer modeling when:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multiple relationship types matter} — Friendship and professional connections behave differently

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node roles vary by context} — A hub in work network may be peripheral in hobby network

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer interactions are important} — Transportation failures in one mode affect others

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Temporal evolution matters} — Relationships change over time

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{System\sphinxhyphen{}level properties emerge} — Cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer dependencies affect resilience

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{Choosing a Modeling Approach}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:choosing-a-modeling-approach}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ask these questions:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layers vs. attributes?} If relationships have different \sphinxstyleemphasis{types} \(\rightarrow\) use layers. If they vary only in \sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} \(\rightarrow\) use edge attributes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Same or different nodes?} Same entities in all layers \(\rightarrow\) multiplex. Different entity types \(\rightarrow\) heterogeneous.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Coupling strength?} Identity coupling only \(\rightarrow\) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega=1.0}}. Nodes can differ \(\rightarrow\) lower omega.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Temporal structure?} Yes \(\rightarrow\) time\sphinxhyphen{}sliced layers. No \(\rightarrow\) aggregate into static network.

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{What Goes Wrong When You Flatten}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:what-goes-wrong-when-you-flatten}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Community structure destroyed:} Flattening can create spurious bridges between groups that are distinct in the layer structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Centrality becomes misleading:} A researcher with 2 coauthors and 500 Twitter followers has degree 502 when flattened, but academic influence is only 2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Path analysis fails:} Email \(\rightarrow\) meeting transitions matter for information flow but are invisible in a flattened network.


\subsubsection{Common Pitfalls}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:common-pitfalls}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Over\sphinxhyphen{}aggregating} — Combining layers that should stay separate

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Under\sphinxhyphen{}aggregating} — Too many sparse layers (use edge weights instead)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Ignoring coupling} — Treating layers as independent when nodes correspond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Wrong coupling strength} — Too high forces artificial consistency; too low loses information

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Mismatched identifiers} — Same entity must have same ID across layers

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Key Terminology}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:key-terminology}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges} — Within a single layer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges} — Between layers (often identity edges connecting same node)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs} — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node\_id, layer\_id)}} tuples, the fundamental unit

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix} — Block matrix encoding both intra\sphinxhyphen{} and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections

\end{itemize}

\subsection{The py3plex Core Model}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{In which we look under the hood at how py3plex represents multilayer networks, understand the node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair representation, and learn to work with the supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix.}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
In the previous chapter, you learned \sphinxstyleemphasis{what} multilayer networks are conceptually. Now we’ll see \sphinxstyleemphasis{how} py3plex represents them in code—and why these design choices matter for your analysis.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Network Types: Multilayer vs Multiplex}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:network-types-multilayer-vs-multiplex}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex supports two network types that determine how layers and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections are handled:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer Networks} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network\_type=\textquotesingle{}multilayer\textquotesingle{}}}, default)

\sphinxAtStartPar
General multilayer networks where each layer can have a different set of nodes. No automatic coupling edges are created.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use when layers represent different node types (e.g., authors, papers, venues)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use when nodes naturally appear in only some layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges must be explicitly added

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Heterogeneous network: authors and papers are different node types}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{multilayer}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{source}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{author1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{target}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{paper1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
     \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{source\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{authors}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{target\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{papers}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multiplex Networks} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network\_type=\textquotesingle{}multiplex\textquotesingle{}}})

\sphinxAtStartPar
Special case where all layers share the same set of nodes but with different relationship types. After loading, coupling edges are automatically created between each node and its counterparts in other layers.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use when the same entities (people, cities) are connected via multiple relationship types

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Coupling edges are auto\sphinxhyphen{}generated with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{type=\textquotesingle{}coupling\textquotesingle{}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Filter coupling edges using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{get\_edges(multiplex\_edges=False)}}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Social network: same people, different relationship types}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{multiplex}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends\PYGZus{}and\PYGZus{}colleagues.edges}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{multiplex\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Coupling edges are auto\PYGZhy{}created between (Alice, friends) \PYGZlt{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{} (Alice, colleagues)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Get only explicit edges (exclude auto\PYGZhy{}coupling)}
\PYG{n}{explicit\PYGZus{}edges} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{multiplex\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Get all edges including coupling}
\PYG{n}{all\PYGZus{}edges} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{multiplex\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsubsection{The \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{multi\_layer\_network}} Class}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:the-multi-layer-network-class}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The central data structure in py3plex is the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{multi\_layer\_network}} class, which provides a high\sphinxhyphen{}level API for working with multilayer networks while maintaining full compatibility with NetworkX.


\paragraph{Basic Structure}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:basic-structure}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Create a multilayer network}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} The underlying NetworkX graph}
\PYG{n}{nx\PYGZus{}graph} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} MultiDiGraph or MultiGraph}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Layer management}
\PYG{n}{layers} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}layers}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} List of layer names}
\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}map} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}name\PYGZus{}map}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Layer name to ID mapping}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Key Components}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:key-components}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1. Core NetworkX Graph}

\sphinxAtStartPar
At its heart, py3plex uses a NetworkX \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiDiGraph}} (for directed networks) or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiGraph}} (for undirected networks) to store all nodes and edges.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Access the underlying graph}
\PYG{n}{G} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Use any NetworkX function}
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{networkx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{nx}
\PYG{n}{betweenness} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{betweenness\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2. Layer Encoding}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Nodes are internally encoded as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node\_id, layer\_id)}} tuples to distinguish the same logical node across different layers.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Node \PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{} in layer \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{} is stored as (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{})}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Access all node\PYGZhy{}layer pairs}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}pair} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}pair}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), ...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3. Layer Mapping}

\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex maintains bidirectional mappings between layer names and internal layer IDs for efficient lookups.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Get layer mapping}
\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}map} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}name\PYGZus{}map}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} \PYGZob{}\PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}: 0, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}: 1, ...\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{4. Attributes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Node and edge attributes are stored directly in the underlying NetworkX graph and can be accessed and modified using standard NetworkX patterns.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Add node with attributes}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{age}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{30}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Add edge with attributes}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{weight}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.8}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{type}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{close}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Internal Representation}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:internal-representation}}

\paragraph{Node\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Pairs}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:node-layer-pairs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The key concept in py3plex’s internal model is the \sphinxstylestrong{node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair}: a tuple \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node\_id, layer\_id)}} that uniquely identifies a node in a specific layer.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Same logical node, different layers}
\PYG{n}{alice\PYGZus{}friends} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{alice\PYGZus{}colleagues} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} These are treated as different nodes internally}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{alice\PYGZus{}friends}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{alice\PYGZus{}colleagues}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This representation allows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The same logical entity to appear in multiple layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Different attributes per node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Efficient layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific operations

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Edge Types}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:edge-types}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Intra\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Edges}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inter\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Edges}

\sphinxAtStartPar

    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}

\subsubsection{Supra\sphinxhyphen{}Adjacency Matrix}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:supra-adjacency-matrix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix is a block matrix representation that encodes the entire multilayer network structure.


\paragraph{Mathematical Definition}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:mathematical-definition}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a multilayer network with \(L\) layers, the supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix}
A_1 & C_{12} & \cdots & C_{1L} \\
C_{21} & A_2 & \cdots & C_{2L} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
C_{L1} & C_{L2} & \cdots & A_L
\end{bmatrix}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_\alpha\) is the adjacency matrix of layer \(\alpha\) (intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_{\alpha\beta}\) is the coupling matrix between layers \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections)

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Numeric Example}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:numeric-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider a simple multiplex network with 3 nodes (A, B, C) and 2 layers. In layer 1, A\sphinxhyphen{}B are connected. In layer 2, B\sphinxhyphen{}C are connected. The nodes are the same across layers (multiplex structure).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network structure:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Layer 1:        Layer 2:
A \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} B   C     A   B \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} C
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node ordering:} We order nodes as (A,L1), (B,L1), (C,L1), (A,L2), (B,L2), (C,L2).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer blocks:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Layer 1 adjacency matrix (A\(\sb{\text{1}}\)):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
     A   B   C
A [  0   1   0 ]
B [  1   0   0 ]
C [  0   0   0 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Layer 2 adjacency matrix (A\(\sb{\text{2}}\)):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
     A   B   C
A [  0   0   0 ]
B [  0   0   1 ]
C [  0   1   0 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer coupling blocks (C\(\sb{\text{1}}\)\(\sb{\text{2}}\) and C\(\sb{\text{2}}\)\(\sb{\text{1}}\)):}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a multiplex network, we typically add identity coupling—each node connects to itself across layers:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
C\(\sb{\text{1}}\)\(\sb{\text{2}}\) = C\(\sb{\text{2}}\)\(\sb{\text{1}}\)ᵀ =
     A   B   C
A [  1   0   0 ]
B [  0   1   0 ]
C [  0   0   1 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Full supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix (6×6):}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
          Layer 1        |     Layer 2
       A    B    C       |  A    B    C
L1  A [ 0    1    0      |  1    0    0 ]
    B [ 1    0    0      |  0    1    0 ]
    C [ 0    0    0      |  0    0    1 ]
   \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}|\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}+\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
L2  A [ 1    0    0      |  0    0    0 ]
    B [ 0    1    0      |  0    0    1 ]
    C [ 0    0    1      |  0    1    0 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The diagonal 3×3 blocks are the within\sphinxhyphen{}layer adjacencies (A\(\sb{\text{1}}\) and A\(\sb{\text{2}}\)). The off\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal 3×3 blocks are the coupling matrices (C\(\sb{\text{1}}\)\(\sb{\text{2}}\) and C\(\sb{\text{2}}\)\(\sb{\text{1}}\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What this enables:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer shortest paths:} A path from (A,L1) to (C,L2) must go through B: (A,L1)\(\rightarrow\)(B,L1)\(\rightarrow\)(B,L2)\(\rightarrow\)(C,L2)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectral methods:} Eigenvalues of S capture multilayer structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Matrix operations:} All linear algebra works on the full system

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Construction}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:construction}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} ... add nodes and edges ...}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Get supra\PYGZhy{}adjacency matrix (sparse by default for efficiency)}
\PYG{n}{supra\PYGZus{}adj} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}supra\PYGZus{}adjacency\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparse}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Dense version (for small networks only)}
\PYG{n}{supra\PYGZus{}adj\PYGZus{}dense} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}supra\PYGZus{}adjacency\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparse}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Shape: (total\PYGZus{}nodes, total\PYGZus{}nodes)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} where total\PYGZus{}nodes = sum of nodes across all layers}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Shape: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{supra\PYGZus{}adj}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{shape}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Memory Implications}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:memory-implications}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix has size (N×L)\(\sp{\text{2}}\) where N is nodes per layer and L is layers:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Small network (100 nodes, 3 layers):} 300×300 = 90,000 entries \(\rightarrow\) \textasciitilde{}720 KB dense

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Medium network (1,000 nodes, 5 layers):} 5,000×5,000 = 25 million entries \(\rightarrow\) \textasciitilde{}200 MB dense

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Large network (10,000 nodes, 10 layers):} 100,000×100,000 = 10 billion entries \(\rightarrow\) impossible dense

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Always use sparse=True} for networks with more than \textasciitilde{}1,000 total node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs. Sparse matrices only store non\sphinxhyphen{}zero entries, reducing memory from O(N\(\sp{\text{2}}\)L\(\sp{\text{2}}\)) to O(edges + coupling).


\paragraph{Visualization}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:visualization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Visualize the supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix structure:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{random\PYGZus{}generators}
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{matplotlib}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{pyplot}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{plt}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Generate a small multilayer network}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{random\PYGZus{}generators}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{random\PYGZus{}multilayer\PYGZus{}ER}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{num\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{num\PYGZus{}layers}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{probability}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{directed}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}
\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Visualize the supra\PYGZhy{}adjacency matrix}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{visualize\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{display}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}

The visualization shows the block structure with:

\subsubsection{How py3plex Uses NetworkX Under the Hood}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:how-py3plex-uses-networkx-under-the-hood}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex is built on top of NetworkX, using it as the storage and algorithm backend. Understanding this architecture helps you leverage the full NetworkX ecosystem.


\paragraph{The Role of MultiGraph/MultiDiGraph}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:the-role-of-multigraph-multidigraph}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Internally, py3plex stores all nodes and edges in a single NetworkX \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiGraph}} (for undirected) or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiDiGraph}} (for directed networks). The multilayer structure is encoded through the node representation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} What you write in py3plex:}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{list}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} What\PYGZsq{}s actually stored in NetworkX:}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Nodes: (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}),}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}        (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{})}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Edges: ((\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{})),}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}        ((\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}))}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{All NetworkX algorithms work directly} on the underlying graph

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer tuples are just nodes} to NetworkX—it doesn’t “know” about layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Attributes are stored as NetworkX attributes} and persist across operations

\end{enumerate}


\paragraph{Attribute Propagation}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:attribute-propagation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you add nodes or edges with attributes, they’re stored in the NetworkX graph:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Node attributes}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{age}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{30}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{role}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{admin}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Edge attributes}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{weight}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.8}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{type}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{close}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Attributes are preserved when you:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Extract subnetworks (filtered nodes keep their attributes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Iterate over nodes/edges with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data=True}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Save and load networks (in formats that support attributes)

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Using NetworkX Functions Directly}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:using-networkx-functions-directly}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Because \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network.core\_network}} is a standard NetworkX graph, you can use any NetworkX function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{networkx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{nx}

\PYG{n}{G} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Standard NetworkX algorithms}
\PYG{n}{betweenness} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{betweenness\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{pagerank} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pagerank}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{components} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{connected\PYGZus{}components}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{to\PYGZus{}undirected}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Shortest paths (work across layers if inter\PYGZhy{}layer edges exist)}
\PYG{n}{path} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{shortest\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Community detection (treats node\PYGZhy{}layer pairs as nodes)}
\PYG{n}{communities} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{community}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{louvain\PYGZus{}communities}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Caveat:} NetworkX doesn’t know about layer semantics. It treats (‘Alice’, ‘friends’) and (‘Alice’, ‘colleagues’) as unrelated nodes. py3plex’s multilayer algorithms add the layer\sphinxhyphen{}aware logic.


\subsubsection{Design Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:design-trade-offs}}

\paragraph{Node\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Pairs vs. Alternative Representations}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:node-layer-pairs-vs-alternative-representations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex’s node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair representation is one of several possible designs. Here’s why it was chosen:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Alternative 1: Separate graphs per layer}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Instead of py3plex:}
\PYG{n}{layer1} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Graph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{layer2} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Graph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{layer1}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{layer2}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Pros:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Simple, familiar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Easy layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific analysis

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cons:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
No representation of inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Manual bookkeeping for cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer operations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Can’t compute multilayer paths or centrality directly

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Alternative 2: Single graph with edge type attributes}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Instead of py3plex:}
\PYG{n}{G} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{MultiGraph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Pros:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Single graph structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Edges carry type information

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cons:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nodes can’t have layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific attributes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Same node in different contexts is the same node (can’t have Alice be central in one layer and peripheral in another)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges to the same node are impossible

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{py3plex approach: Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{list}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Pros:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Preserves both intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Allows layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific node attributes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compatible with NetworkX algorithms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enables proper multilayer\sphinxhyphen{}specific operations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Supports identity coupling and cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cons:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Node names are tuples (less intuitive for simple cases)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Memory usage is multiplied by number of layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
NetworkX algorithms treat node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs as independent nodes (need py3plex wrappers for multilayer semantics)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{py3plex’s choice:} The node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair approach was chosen because it correctly models multilayer semantics while maintaining NetworkX compatibility. The downsides (tuple names, memory) are acceptable trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs for the flexibility and correctness gained.


\paragraph{Consequences for Algorithm Implementation}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:consequences-for-algorithm-implementation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair design has implications:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer extraction is subsetting:} To get layer 1, you filter nodes where the layer component equals “layer1”

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Identity coupling is explicit:} Cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges between the same entity must be added explicitly (or automatically in multiplex mode)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Supra\sphinxhyphen{}matrix is derivable:} The supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix can be computed from the graph structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NetworkX algorithms work but need interpretation:} Betweenness on the full graph treats cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges as normal edges

\end{enumerate}


\paragraph{Consequences for I/O}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:consequences-for-i-o}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair representation affects serialization:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Standard formats work:} GraphML, GML can store tuple nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Human\sphinxhyphen{}readable formats need mapping:} Edgelists typically use separate columns for node and layer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Arrow/Parquet are efficient:} Modern columnar formats handle the structure naturally

\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Performance Considerations}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:performance-considerations}}

\paragraph{Sparse vs. Dense Matrices}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:sparse-vs-dense-matrices}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For large networks, always use sparse matrix representations:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Good: Sparse matrix (efficient for large networks)}
\PYG{n}{supra\PYGZus{}adj} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}supra\PYGZus{}adjacency\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparse}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Bad: Dense matrix (memory\PYGZhy{}intensive)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Only use for small networks (\PYGZlt{} 1000 nodes)}
\PYG{n}{supra\PYGZus{}adj\PYGZus{}dense} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}supra\PYGZus{}adjacency\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparse}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Memory Usage}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:memory-usage}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs mean that a node appearing in \(L\) layers occupies \(L\) times the memory of a single\sphinxhyphen{}layer network. For networks with many layers:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific analysis when possible

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use subnetwork extraction to work with smaller portions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Performance and Scalability Best Practices}}}} for optimization strategies

\end{itemize}

\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:tensor-like-indexing}}

You can access nodes and edges using tensor\sphinxhyphen{}like notation:

\subsubsection{Design Principles}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:design-principles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex follows several key design principles:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1. NetworkX Compatibility}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All operations maintain compatibility with NetworkX, allowing seamless use of the rich NetworkX ecosystem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2. Lazy Evaluation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Expensive operations like supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix construction are computed on demand and cached when appropriate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3. Graceful Degradation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional features (like Infomap community detection or advanced visualizations) fail gracefully with informative error messages if dependencies are missing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{4. Extensibility}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The modular design makes it easy to extend py3plex with custom algorithms and visualizations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{5. Flexibility}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiple ways to construct and manipulate networks to suit different workflows and use cases.


\subsubsection{Comparison with Other Representations}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:comparison-with-other-representations}}

\paragraph{Why Node\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Pairs?}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:why-node-layer-pairs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternative representations exist, but py3plex’s node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair approach offers key advantages:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Alternative: Separate graphs per layer}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Drawback:} Loses inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer information, requires manual bookkeeping for cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer operations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Alternative: Single graph with edge type attributes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Drawback:} Cannot distinguish node context across layers, loses layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific node attributes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{py3plex approach: Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Advantages:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Preserves both intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Allows layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific node attributes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compatible with NetworkX algorithms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Efficient for multilayer\sphinxhyphen{}specific operations

\end{itemize}

\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{basic\PYGZus{}stats}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Works immediately}

\subsection{Algorithm Landscape}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:algorithm-landscape}}\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This guide provides a narrative overview of the algorithm families available in py3plex, helping you understand when to use each type of algorithm for multilayer network analysis.


\subsubsection{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex provides algorithms in seven main categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Community Detection} \sphinxhyphen{} Finding groups of densely connected nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Centrality \& Importance} \sphinxhyphen{} Measuring node and edge importance

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network Statistics} \sphinxhyphen{} Computing network\sphinxhyphen{}level and layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific metrics

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Random Walks \& Embeddings} \sphinxhyphen{} Node representations and sampling

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node Ranking \& Classification} \sphinxhyphen{} Ordering and classifying nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Visualization \& Layout} \sphinxhyphen{} Rendering and spatial arrangement

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Benchmarking \& Generation} \sphinxhyphen{} Testing and synthetic network creation

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For detailed parameter lists and API reference, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/algorithm_reference::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Algorithm Roadmap}}}}.


\subsubsection{Community Detection}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:community-detection}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Goal:} Identify groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest of the network.


\paragraph{When to Use}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:when-to-use}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use community detection when you want to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Discover functional modules in biological networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find social groups in multilayer social networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identify topical clusters in citation networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand organizational structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Detect anomalies (nodes that don’t fit any community)

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Algorithm Families}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:algorithm-families}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Modularity\sphinxhyphen{}Based Methods}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Best for:} Fast community detection on large networks

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Louvain} \sphinxhyphen{} Fast, greedy modularity optimization

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Leiden} \sphinxhyphen{} Improved version of Louvain with better stability

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer Louvain} \sphinxhyphen{} Extends Louvain to multiple layers with inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer coupling

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Fast (scales to millions of nodes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Easy to use (minimal parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Resolution limit (may miss small communities)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Stochastic (different runs give different results)

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}louvain}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Single\PYGZhy{}layer Louvain}
\PYG{n}{partition} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}louvain}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{best\PYGZus{}partition}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Multilayer Louvain}
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{multilayer\PYGZus{}modularity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{louvain\PYGZus{}multilayer}
\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{partition} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{louvain\PYGZus{}multilayer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{omega}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Flow\sphinxhyphen{}Based Methods}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Best for:} Finding communities based on information flow

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Infomap} \sphinxhyphen{} Minimizes description length of random walks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Walktrap} \sphinxhyphen{} Based on random walk distances

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Theoretically grounded (information theory)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Finds hierarchical structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Slower than modularity methods

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ May require external binaries

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}wrapper}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Infomap (requires binary)}
\PYG{n}{partition} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}wrapper}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{infomap\PYGZus{}communities}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{binary\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/path/to/infomap}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Overlapping Community Detection}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Best for:} Networks where nodes belong to multiple communities

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NoRC} \sphinxhyphen{} Network of Ranked Communities

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Clique Percolation} \sphinxhyphen{} Based on overlapping cliques

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) More realistic for many real networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Captures multi\sphinxhyphen{}role nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ More complex to interpret

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Computationally expensive

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}wrapper}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} NoRC overlapping communities}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Choosing a Community Detection Method}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:choosing-a-community-detection-method}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use this decision tree:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Do you need overlapping communities?
├─ Yes \(\rightarrow\) NoRC or Clique Percolation
└─ No
   └─ Is your network multilayer?
      ├─ Yes \(\rightarrow\) Multilayer Louvain or Leiden
      └─ No
         └─ What\PYGZsq{}s most important?
            ├─ Speed \(\rightarrow\) Louvain
            ├─ Stability \(\rightarrow\) Leiden
            └─ Theory \(\rightarrow\) Infomap
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\paragraph{Choosing a Centrality Measure}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:choosing-a-centrality-measure}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider these questions:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Local vs. Global?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Local \(\rightarrow\) Degree centrality
\sphinxhyphen{} Global \(\rightarrow\) Closeness or betweenness

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Direct connections or influence?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Direct \(\rightarrow\) Degree
\sphinxhyphen{} Influence \(\rightarrow\) PageRank or eigenvector

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network type?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Directed \(\rightarrow\) PageRank or HITS
\sphinxhyphen{} Undirected \(\rightarrow\) Any method
\sphinxhyphen{} Weighted \(\rightarrow\) Use weight\sphinxhyphen{}aware versions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Computational cost?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Large network \(\rightarrow\) Degree or PageRank (fast)
\sphinxhyphen{} Small network \(\rightarrow\) Betweenness (expensive but informative)

\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Choosing Walk Parameters}

\sphinxstylestrong{walk\_length:}

\item {}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{p (return parameter):}
\begin{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
p \textgreater{} 1: Less likely to return

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
q = 1: Balanced

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{String Syntax Reference}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:string-syntax-reference}}

\paragraph{Basic Structure}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:basic-structure}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
SELECT \PYGZlt{}target\PYGZgt{} [FROM \PYGZlt{}layers\PYGZgt{}] [WHERE \PYGZlt{}conditions\PYGZgt{}] [COMPUTE \PYGZlt{}metrics\PYGZgt{}] [ORDER BY \PYGZlt{}field\PYGZgt{}] [LIMIT \PYGZlt{}n\PYGZgt{}]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Targets}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:targets}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nodes}} — Select nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{edges}} — Select edges (experimental)

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Layer Selection}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:layer-selection}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
FROM layer=\PYGZdq{}layer\PYGZus{}name\PYGZdq{}
FROM layers IN (\PYGZdq{}layer1\PYGZdq{}, \PYGZdq{}layer2\PYGZdq{})
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Conditions}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:conditions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Operators:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{=}} — Equal

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textgreater{}}} — Greater than

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}}} — Less than

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textgreater{}=}} — Greater than or equal

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}=}} — Less than or equal

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{!=}} — Not equal

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Logical operators:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{AND}} — Both conditions must be true

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OR}} — Either condition must be true

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Examples:}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:compute-clause}}

\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{closeness\_centrality}} — Closeness centrality

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clustering}} — Clustering coefficient

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pagerank}} — PageRank score

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{layer\_count}} — Number of layers node appears in

\paragraph{Limitations}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:limitations}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Coverage filtering is currently supported only for \sphinxstylestrong{node queries}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Edge queries with coverage will raise a clear \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DslExecutionError}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Grouping requires computed attributes or inherent node properties (like layer)

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Working with Results}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:working-with-results}}

\paragraph{Result Object}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:result-object}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Query results are dictionaries mapping nodes to their computed attributes:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{Q}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{degree}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Access individual node}
\PYG{n}{node} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{degree} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{result}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{node}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{degree}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Iterate}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{node}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{data} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{result}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{items}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{node}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{dsl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{register\PYGZus{}operator}

\subsubsection{Performance Considerations}
\label{\detokenize{reference/dsl_reference:performance-considerations}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compute metrics once:} Don’t recompute in multiple queries

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Filter early:} Use WHERE before COMPUTE

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limit results:} Use LIMIT for large networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific:} Query single layers when possible

\end{enumerate}

Bases: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{object}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Main class for multilayer network analysis and manipulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This class provides a comprehensive toolkit for creating, analyzing, and
visualizing multilayer networks where nodes can exist in multiple layers
and edges can connect nodes within or across layers.
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Supported Network Types (network\_type parameter):}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{multilayer} (default): General multilayer networks with arbitrary
layer structure. Each layer can have a different set of nodes.
Suitable for heterogeneous networks (e.g., authors\sphinxhyphen{}papers\sphinxhyphen{}venues)
or networks where nodes naturally appear in only some layers.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{multiplex}: Special case where all layers share the same node set
but with different edge types. After loading a network, automatic
coupling edges are created between each node and its counterparts
in other layers. Suitable for social networks with multiple
relationship types (e.g., friend, colleague, family layers).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Choosing the Right Network Type:}
\sphinxlineitem{Key Features:}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dict\sphinxhyphen{}based API for adding nodes and edges (see add\_nodes() and add\_edges())

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
NetworkX interoperability via to\_networkx() and from\_networkx()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiple I/O formats (edgelist, GML, GraphML, gpickle, etc.)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Visualization methods for multilayer layouts

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Community detection and centrality analysis

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Random walk and embedding generation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Hypergraph Support:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This class does NOT natively support true hypergraphs (edges connecting
more than two nodes). For hypergraph\sphinxhyphen{}like structures, consider:
\sphinxhyphen{} Using bipartite projections (nodes and hyperedges as separate node types)
\sphinxhyphen{} The incidence gadget encoding via to\_homogeneous\_hypergraph()
\sphinxhyphen{} External hypergraph libraries with conversion utilities

\end{description}
\subsubsection*{Notes}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nodes in multilayer networks are represented as (node\_id, layer) tuples

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use add\_nodes() and add\_edges() with dict format for easiest interaction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
See examples/ directory for usage patterns and best practices

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Add edges to the multilayer network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method supports multiple input formats for specifying edges between nodes
in different layers. The most common format is dict\sphinxhyphen{}based.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection*{Notes}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges, use the same layer for source\_type and target\_type

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges, use different layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Edge weights default to 1.0 if not specified

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Add nodes to the multilayer network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Nodes in a multilayer network are identified by both their ID and the layer
they belong to. This method adds nodes using a dict\sphinxhyphen{}based format.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{node\_dict\_list}} \textendash{} Node data as a dict or list of dicts (see format below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{input\_type}} \textendash{} Format of node data (currently only ‘dict’ is supported)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Returns self for method chaining

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
self

\end{description}\end{quote}
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Dict Format:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\color{red}\bfseries{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}{\color{red}\bfseries{}\textasciigrave{}}python
\{
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
‘source’: ‘node\_id’,    \# Node identifier (can be string or number)
‘type’: ‘layer\_name’,   \# Layer this node belongs to
‘weight’: 1.0,          \# Optional: node weight/importance
‘label’: ‘display’      \# Optional: display label
\# … any other node attributes
\end{quote}

\end{description}

\subsubsection*{Notes}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The same node ID can exist in multiple layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Each (node\_id, layer) combination is treated as a unique node

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional attributes beyond ‘source’ and ‘type’ are preserved

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nodes must be added before edges referencing them

\end{itemize}

\end{fulllineitems}\end{savenotes}

{{ $\rightarrow$ Dict\DUrole{p}{{[}}str\DUrole{p}{,}\DUrole{w}{ }Any\DUrole{p}{{]}}}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute Ollivier\sphinxhyphen{}Ricci curvature on the multilayer network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method provides flexible computation of Ollivier\sphinxhyphen{}Ricci curvature
at different levels of the multilayer network:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{core mode}: Compute curvature on the aggregated (flattened) network

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{layers mode}: Compute curvature separately for each layer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{supra mode}: Compute curvature on the full supra\sphinxhyphen{}graph including
both intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges

\end{itemize}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{mode}} \textendash{} Scope of computation. Options: “core”, “layers”, “supra”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{layers}} \textendash{} List of layer identifiers to process (only for mode=”layers”).
If None, all layers are processed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{alpha}} \textendash{} Ollivier\sphinxhyphen{}Ricci parameter in {[}0, 1{]} controlling the mass
distribution. Default: 0.5.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{weight\_attr}} \textendash{} Name of edge attribute containing weights. Default: “weight”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{curvature\_attr}} \textendash{} Name of edge attribute to store curvature values.
Default: “ricciCurvature”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{verbose}} \textendash{} Verbosity level. Options: “INFO”, “DEBUG”, “ERROR”. Default: “ERROR”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{backend\_kwargs}} \textendash{} Additional keyword arguments for OllivierRicci constructor.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{inplace}} \textendash{} If True, update internal graphs. If False, return new graphs
without modifying the network. Default: True.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{interlayer\_weight}} \textendash{} Weight for inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer coupling edges (only for
mode=”supra”). Default: 1.0.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dictionary mapping scope identifiers to NetworkX graphs with computed
curvatures:
\sphinxhyphen{} mode=”core”: \{“core”: graph\_with\_curvature\}
\sphinxhyphen{} mode=”layers”: \{layer\_id: graph\_with\_curvature, …\}
\sphinxhyphen{} mode=”supra”: \{“supra”: supra\_graph\_with\_curvature\}

\sphinxlineitem{Raises}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{RicciBackendNotAvailable}} \textendash{} If GraphRicciCurvature is not installed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ValueError}} \textendash{} If mode is invalid or layers contains invalid identifiers.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute Ollivier\sphinxhyphen{}Ricci flow on the multilayer network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Ricci flow iteratively adjusts edge weights based on their Ricci curvature,
effectively revealing and enhancing community structure. After Ricci flow,
edges with negative curvature (community boundaries) have reduced weights,
while edges with positive curvature have increased weights.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{mode}} \textendash{} Scope of computation. Options: “core”, “layers”, “supra”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{layers}} \textendash{} List of layer identifiers to process (only for mode=”layers”).
If None, all layers are processed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{alpha}} \textendash{} Ollivier\sphinxhyphen{}Ricci parameter in {[}0, 1{]}. Default: 0.5.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{iterations}} \textendash{} Number of Ricci flow iterations. Default: 10.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{method}} \textendash{} Ricci flow method. Options: “OTD” (Optimal Transport Distance,
recommended), “ATD” (Average Transport Distance). Default: “OTD”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{weight\_attr}} \textendash{} Name of edge attribute containing weights. After Ricci flow,
these weights are updated to reflect the flow metric.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{curvature\_attr}} \textendash{} Name of edge attribute for curvature values.
Default: “ricciCurvature”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{verbose}} \textendash{} Verbosity level. Options: “INFO”, “DEBUG”, “ERROR”. Default: “ERROR”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{backend\_kwargs}} \textendash{} Additional keyword arguments for OllivierRicci constructor.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{inplace}} \textendash{} If True, update internal graphs. If False, return new graphs.
Default: True.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{interlayer\_weight}} \textendash{} Weight for inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer coupling edges (only for
mode=”supra”). Default: 1.0.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dictionary mapping scope identifiers to NetworkX graphs with Ricci flow
applied:
\sphinxhyphen{} mode=”core”: \{“core”: graph\_with\_flow\}
\sphinxhyphen{} mode=”layers”: \{layer\_id: graph\_with\_flow, …\}
\sphinxhyphen{} mode=”supra”: \{“supra”: supra\_graph\_with\_flow\}

\sphinxlineitem{Raises}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{RicciBackendNotAvailable}} \textendash{} If GraphRicciCurvature is not installed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ValueError}} \textendash{} If mode is invalid or layers contains invalid identifiers.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

Convert a temporal edge DataFrame to edge tuple list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Extracts edges from a pandas DataFrame with temporal/activity information
and converts them to a list of edge tuples suitable for network construction.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{edge\_df}} \textendash{} pandas DataFrame with columns:
\sphinxhyphen{} node\_first: Source node identifier
\sphinxhyphen{} node\_second: Target node identifier
\sphinxhyphen{} layer\_name: Layer identifier

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{List of edge tuples in format:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(node\_first, node\_second, layer\_first, layer\_second, weight)
where weight is always 1

\end{description}


\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
list

\end{description}\end{quote}
\subsubsection*{Notes}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All values are converted to strings

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All edges are assigned weight=1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Both source and target are assumed to be in the same layer

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Execute a DSL query on this multilayer network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a convenience method that provides first\sphinxhyphen{}class access to the
py3plex DSL (Domain\sphinxhyphen{}Specific Language) for querying multilayer networks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Supports both SELECT and MATCH queries:
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{SELECT queries:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
net.execute\_query(‘SELECT nodes WHERE layer=”transport”’)
net.execute\_query(‘SELECT * FROM nodes IN LAYER “ppi” WHERE degree \textgreater{} 10’)

\sphinxlineitem{MATCH queries (Cypher\sphinxhyphen{}like):}
\sphinxAtStartPar
net.execute\_query(‘MATCH (g:Gene)\sphinxhyphen{}{[}r{]}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}(t:Gene) RETURN g, t’)
net.execute\_query(‘MATCH (a)\sphinxhyphen{}{[}e{]}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}(b) IN LAYER “ppi” WHERE a.degree \textgreater{} 5 RETURN a, b’)

\end{description}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{query}} \textendash{} DSL query string

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For SELECT queries: ‘nodes’ or ‘edges’ list, ‘count’, optional ‘computed’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For MATCH queries: ‘bindings’ list, ‘count’, ‘type’

\end{itemize}


\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dictionary containing query results

\sphinxlineitem{Raises}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/api_index:py3plex.dsl.DSLSyntaxError}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{DSLSyntaxError}}}}} \textendash{} If query syntax is invalid

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/api_index:py3plex.dsl.DSLExecutionError}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{DSLExecutionError}}}}} \textendash{} If query cannot be executed

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

the original layers based on cycle lengths (prime numbers).

\index{get\_edges() (py3plex.core.multinet.multi\_layer\_network method)@\spxentry{get\_edges()}\spxextra{py3plex.core.multinet.multi\_layer\_network method}}

\begin{savenotes}\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{reference/api_index:py3plex.core.multinet.multi_layer_network.get_edges}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{get\_edges}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{data}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{bool}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{default_value}{False}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{multiplex\_edges}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{bool}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{default_value}{False}}}
{{ $\rightarrow$ Any}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Iterate over edges in the network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method behaves differently based on the network\_type:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{multilayer}: Returns all edges without filtering.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{multiplex}: By default, filters out coupling edges (auto\sphinxhyphen{}generated
inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges connecting each node to itself in other layers).
Set multiplex\_edges=True to include coupling edges.

\end{itemize}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{data}} \textendash{} If True, return edge data along with edge tuples

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{multiplex\_edges}} \textendash{} If True, include coupling edges in multiplex networks.
Only relevant when network\_type=’multiplex’. Coupling edges are
automatically added to connect each node to its counterparts
in other layers.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Yields}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Edge tuples, optionally with data. For multiplex networks with
multiplex\_edges=False, coupling edges are excluded.

\sphinxlineitem{Raises}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ValueError}} \textendash{} If network\_type is not ‘multilayer’ or ‘multiplex’.

\end{description}\end{quote}
\subsubsection*{Examples}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n}{net} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{multilayer}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n}{net}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}

\index{get\_tensor() (py3plex.core.multinet.multi\_layer\_network method)@\spxentry{get\_tensor()}\spxextra{py3plex.core.multinet.multi\_layer\_network method}}

\begin{savenotes}\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{reference/api_index:py3plex.core.multinet.multi_layer_network.get_tensor}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{get\_tensor}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{sparsity\_type}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{\textquotesingle{}bsr\textquotesingle{}}}}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Get sparse tensor representation of the multilayer network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Returns the supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix in the specified sparse format.
This method provides a tensor\sphinxhyphen{}like view of the multilayer network,
useful for mathematical analysis and matrix\sphinxhyphen{}based algorithms.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sparsity\_type}} \textendash{} Sparse matrix format to use. Options include:
\sphinxhyphen{} ‘bsr’ (default): Block Sparse Row format
\sphinxhyphen{} ‘csr’: Compressed Sparse Row format
\sphinxhyphen{} ‘csc’: Compressed Sparse Column format
\sphinxhyphen{} ‘coo’: Coordinate format
\sphinxhyphen{} ‘lil’: List of Lists format
\sphinxhyphen{} ‘dok’: Dictionary of Keys format

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix in specified format

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
scipy.sparse matrix

\end{description}\end{quote}
\subsubsection*{Example}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n}{net} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n}{tensor} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{net}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}tensor}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparsity\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{csr}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{tensor}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{shape}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The returned matrix is the same as get\_supra\_adjacency\_matrix(mtype=’sparse’)
but with control over the specific sparse format used.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\end{fulllineitems}\end{savenotes}
